title: Functor comparison and universal evaluation from first-projection open loci
statement: Let $Z\to S$ and $X\to S$ be morphisms of schemes [def-pc-scheme], put $Z_T=Z\times_ST$, $X_T=X\times_ST$ [def-pc-fibre-product], and write $\mathcal M(T)=\operatorname{Hom}_T(Z_T,X_T)$ [def-sfb-relative-morphisms-presheaf]. Let $F$ be a presheaf of sets on $S$-schemes such that $F(T)$ is a collection of closed subschemes $j_D:D\hookrightarrow Z_T\times_TX_T$ [def-weil-closed-immersion], with restriction maps given by pullback of closed subschemes. Assume that assigning the actual graph $\Gamma_f=(\mathrm{id},f)$ gives a natural transformation $\gamma:\mathcal M\to F$. Write $k_D=\operatorname{pr}_1\circ j_D$ and $l_D=\operatorname{pr}_2\circ j_D$. Then $\gamma_T$ is injective and $D$ is in its image exactly when $k_D$ is an isomorphism; the unique inverse-image morphism is $l_D\circ k_D^{-1}$. For every $D\in F(T)$, with $h_T(T')=\operatorname{Hom}_S(T',T)$ [def-pc-representable-functor], the functor $h_T\times_F\mathcal M$ is naturally identified with the functor of maps $h:T'\to T$ for which $k_{D_{T'}}$ is an isomorphism. Suppose, in addition, that for every $D\in F(T)$ an open subscheme $U_D\subseteq T$ [def-weil-open-immersion] satisfies, for every $h:T'\to T$, that $k_{D_{T'}}$ is an isomorphism if and only if $h$ factors through $U_D$. Then $h_T\times_F\mathcal M\cong h_{U_D}$ over $h_T$, so $\gamma$ is representable by open immersions [def-pc-open-subfunctor]. If $H$ represents $F$, with universal closed family $D_H$, then $M=U_{D_H}\subseteq H$ represents $\mathcal M$ and its inclusion represents $\gamma$. The evaluation $Z_M\to X_M$ is $l_{D_M}\circ k_{D_M}^{-1}$, where $D_M=D_H\times_HM$. Every $a:T\to M$ pulls this evaluation back to the morphism classified by $a$. Under every $T_0\to T$, one has $U_{D_{T_0}}=T_0\times_TU_D$ as open subschemes and $(k_D^{-1})_{T_0}=(k_{D_{T_0}})^{-1}$ wherever these inverses exist; hence these identifications and evaluation commute with arbitrary base change.

proof.text: For an actual graph $\Gamma_f=(\mathrm{id},f)$ the first projection restricted to the graph is the identity of $Z_T$, and the second is $f$, by the defining equations of the fibre product. Thus its first projection is invertible and $f=l_{\Gamma_f}\circ k_{\Gamma_f}^{-1}$. Equality of two closed graph subschemes identifies their inclusions and projections over $Z_T\times_TX_T$, so this formula recovers the same morphism from either. This proves injectivity of $\gamma_T$.

proof.text: Conversely, if $k_D:D\to Z_T$ is invertible, set $f=l_D\circ k_D^{-1}$. This is a $T$-morphism, since both projections of $j_D$ are over $T$. The morphisms $j_D\circ k_D^{-1}$ and $(\mathrm{id},f)$ to $Z_T\times_TX_T$ have the same first projection $\mathrm{id}$ and the same second projection $f$, so they are equal by the fibre-product universal property. Hence $k_D^{-1}$ identifies the inclusion of $D$ with the actual graph of $f$, as closed subschemes, not just as sets. This proves the image criterion and, with step 1, uniqueness.

proof.text: Fix $D\in F(T)$. The element $D$ defines $\delta_D:h_T\to F$ by $\delta_D(h)=h^*D$; the Yoneda bijection identifies this with the map corresponding to $D$. On an $S$-scheme $T\prime$, the set pullback $h_T\times_F\mathcal M$ consists exactly of pairs $(h,f)$ with $h:T\prime\to T$ and $\Gamma_f=h^*D$. Under further pullback $u:T\prime\prime\to T\prime$ it sends $(h,f)$ to $(h\circ u,u^*f)$, by the assumed naturality of $\gamma$. Steps 1 and 2 show that forgetting $f$ is a bijection onto the maps $h$ for which $k_{h^*D}$ is invertible, with inverse $h\mapsto(h,l_{h^*D}\circ k_{h^*D}^{-1})$. Forgetting commutes with restrictions by the displayed formula, so its bijective inverse is natural too.

proof.text: An open inclusion $i:U\hookrightarrow T$ is a monomorphism: the underlying map of spaces is injective and the structure sheaf on $U$ is the restriction of that on $T$, so a map to $U$ over a fixed map to $T$ has its continuous map and its sheaf map uniquely prescribed. Thus $\operatorname{Hom}_S(T\prime,U)\to\operatorname{Hom}_S(T\prime,T)$ identifies its source with the maps factoring through $U$. Apply this with $U=U_D$. The assumed universal property of $U_D$ identifies this image with exactly the image in step 3. The resulting bijections $h_{U_D}\cong h_T\times_F\mathcal M$ are natural and preserve the map to $h_T$. Identifying $\mathcal M$ with its image by injectivity, this is precisely representability by open immersions in the cited definition.

source.place: Tags 0D1A and 0D1B, quot-lemma-Mor-into-Hilb, last proof paragraph, and quot-lemma-Mor-into-Hilb-open, graph criterion; explicit functorial consequences.

proof.text: Choose the representing isomorphism $h_H\cong F$ and let $D_H$ be the image of $\mathrm{id}_H$. Naturality (equivalently the Yoneda formula) says that $b:T\to H$ corresponds to $b^*D_H$. Put $i:M=U_{D_H}\hookrightarrow H$. Step 4 with $T=H$ gives $h_M\cong h_H\times_F\mathcal M$. Projection from the latter pullback to $\mathcal M$ is an isomorphism: on each test scheme its inverse sends $f$ to $(b_f,f)$, where $b_f$ is the unique map corresponding under $h_H\cong F$ to $\gamma(f)$. These formulas commute with restrictions. Consequently $M$ represents $\mathcal M$, and the induced map $h_M\to F$ is the one represented by its inclusion into $H$.

proof.text: The inclusion $i:M\to H$ factors through $U_{D_H}$, so the hypothesis applied to $i$ says that $k_{D_M}$ is an isomorphism, where $D_M=i^*D_H$. Step 2 recovers the morphism $e=l_{D_M}\circ k_{D_M}^{-1}:Z_M\to X_M$ with graph $D_M$. Under the isomorphism in step 5, the element $\mathrm{id}_M\in h_M(M)$ corresponds to this $e$: its graph is the family classified by $i$, and injectivity of $\gamma_M$ ensures equality. For $a:T\to M$, naturality of this representing isomorphism therefore gives precisely $a^*e$ as the morphism classified by $a$.

proof.text: For completeness the inverse-projection formula itself commutes with arbitrary pullback. If $k_D$ is invertible and $h:T_0\to T$, form the induced morphisms $k_{D,T_0}$ and $(k_D^{-1})_{T_0}$ using the fibre-product universal property. Their two composites have the same two projections as the appropriate identity maps: on the first projections they are the pullbacks of $k_Dk_D^{-1}=\mathrm{id}$ or $k_D^{-1}k_D=\mathrm{id}$, and on the base projection they are identities. Uniqueness in the universal property makes both composites identities. Thus $(k_D^{-1})_{T_0}=(k_{D_{T_0}})^{-1}$ under the canonical identifications. The same uniqueness shows that pullback preserves composition, whence $(l_D\circ k_D^{-1})_{T_0}=l_{D_{T_0}}\circ(k_{D_{T_0}})^{-1}$. For two successive base changes the canonical identifications agree, since their composites with every projection agree.

source.place: Tags 0D1A and 0D1B, quot-lemma-Mor-into-Hilb, last proof paragraph, and quot-lemma-Mor-into-Hilb-open, graph criterion; explicit functorial consequences.

proof.text: Let $h:T_0\to T$, $V=U_{D_{T_0}}$, and $W=T_0\times_TU_D$, with projection $w:W\to T_0$. By the fibre-product universal property, maps to $W$ over $T_0$ are exactly maps whose composite to $T$ factors through $U_D$. Equivalently, $W$ is the restriction of $T_0$ to $h^{-1}|U_D|$, with its restricted structure sheaf, hence is an open subscheme. For any $g:R\to T_0$, the presheaf pullback law identifies $g^*D_{T_0}$ with $(h\circ g)^*D$. The assumed universal properties therefore say $g$ factors through $V$ if and only if $h\circ g$ factors through $U_D$, if and only if $g$ factors through $W$. Taking $g$ first to be the inclusion of $V$ and then $w$ produces maps $V\to W$ and $W\to V$ over $T_0$. Their composites are identities by uniqueness of factorization through an open inclusion, proved in step 4. Thus these opens coincide as open subschemes. Together with step 7 and the explicit pair/factorization maps in steps 3--6, this proves all the claimed base-change compatibilities.
